[S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)\\n\\n### Observed infant symptoms\\nLactMed reports the following observations:\\n\\n- In a telephone follow-up of 25 nursing mothers, 3 reported infant diarrhea; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that study. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)\\n- In a study of 40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breastmilk, 2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)\\n- In a study comparing amoxicillin with a macrolide antibiotic, reactions occurred in 8.3% of amoxicillin-exposed infants and included rash and somnolence. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)\\n- A separate case involved an infant who developed generalized urticaria after breastfeeding when the mother was receiving amoxicillin/clavulanate and gentamicin. The drug responsible could not be determined; the report considered amoxicillin/clavulanate the more likely cause. The urticaria appeared after each of two breastfeeding episodes, but the exact elapsed timing between the exposure changes and later follow-up is not fully specified. [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)\\n- Another report described mild diarrhea in an 11-month-old whose mother was taking amoxicillin along with acetaminophen plus codeine; the report rated the association possible or probable. [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)\\n- In a study of 25 breastfeeding mothers and infants older than 4 weeks, no infant adverse effects were reported. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)\\n\\n### Advice to monitor\\nThe retrieved LactMed record describes a study in which mothers monitored infants for tongue changes, feeding difficulties, stool changes, diaper rash, skin rash, weight change, and jaundice. request.question: What does LactMed report about amoxicillin in breastfed babies? Separate observed symptoms from advice to monitor, and explain uncertainty. Do not give a dose.

response.answer:
## LactMed: amoxicillin in breastfed infants

### Measured exposure
- In a study of 6 women, reported milk concentrations were **0.69 mg/L** (range **0.46–0.88 mg/L**) at 4 hours and **0.81 mg/L** (range **0.39–1.3 mg/L**) at 5 hours after administration. These are milk measurements.  
- **Infant drug levels:** relevant published information was not found in the LactMed record as of its revision date; the specimen type is therefore not available. [S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)

### Observed infant symptoms
LactMed reports the following observations:

- In a telephone follow-up of 25 nursing mothers, 3 reported infant diarrhea; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that study. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)
- In a study of 40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breastmilk, 2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)
- In a study comparing amoxicillin with a macrolide antibiotic, reactions occurred in 8.3% of amoxicillin-exposed infants and included rash and somnolence. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)
- A separate case involved an infant who developed generalized urticaria after breastfeeding when the mother was receiving amoxicillin/clavulanate and gentamicin. The drug responsible could not be determined; the report considered amoxicillin/clavulanate the more likely cause. The urticaria appeared after each of two breastfeeding episodes, but the exact elapsed timing between the exposure changes and later follow-up is not fully specified. [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)
- Another report described mild diarrhea in an 11-month-old whose mother was taking amoxicillin along with acetaminophen plus codeine; the report rated the association possible or probable. [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)
- In a study of 25 breastfeeding mothers and infants older than 4 weeks, no infant adverse effects were reported. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)

### Advice to monitor
The retrieved LactMed record describes a study in which mothers monitored infants for tongue changes, feeding difficulties, stool changes, diaper rash, skin rash, weight change, and jaundice. It does **not** provide a separate explicit LactMed recommendation to monitor those symptoms. A symptom included in a study-monitoring protocol is not evidence that it occurred or that LactMed advised families to watch for it.

### Uncertainty
LactMed states that reported rash and gastrointestinal effects had not been adequately evaluated. The retrieved record does not establish a study count, and its “no adverse effects reported” statement does not establish that such effects are absent. The infant-level section reports that relevant published information was not found.

This was a bounded LactMed extract: all expected sections were returned without marked truncation, but it is not a guarantee that no other evidence exists. The record was revised **2026-06-15** and came from an NCBI package published **2026-10-22**. [S12](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

The MCP server notes that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician; this is a server notice, not a LactMed statement.

request.question: For sumatriptan during breastfeeding, what was measured in milk and what was actually observed in infants? If those are different kinds of evidence, explain that. No personal medication advice.

response.answer:
## Measured exposure in milk

LactMed reported these **sumatriptan concentrations in breast milk**:

- **Peak milk concentration:** average **87.2 mcg/L** (range **62–113 mcg/L**), measured in five breastfeeding women; sampling peaked about **2.5 hours** after exposure.  
- In a separate group of seven breastfeeding women, **peak milk concentration:** average **59.3 mcg/L** (range **24.6–112.8 mcg/L**), occurring **2–4 hours** after exposure.  
- In that group, the **average milk concentration** was **23.2 mcg/L** (range **7.7–50.6 mcg/L**).

These are measurements in **milk**, not measurements from an infant specimen. LactMed states that relevant published information on **infant levels** was not found as of the record’s revision date. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/) [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8866921/) [S2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33730376/)

## What was observed in infants

LactMed reports manufacturer correspondence concerning **three women who used sumatriptan while breastfeeding**; none reported adverse effects in their infants. The record does not provide infant drug concentrations or detailed clinical assessments for those infants. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

## Why these are different kinds of evidence

Milk concentrations measure **drug exposure in the milk compartment**. Infant observations describe **reported clinical outcomes**. A milk concentration does not establish an infant’s specimen concentration or a clinical effect, and the limited report of no reported adverse effects does not establish that infant exposure was absent or that all possible outcomes were assessed. Thus, the retrieved evidence includes quantitative milk measurements but no reported infant-level drug measurements and only limited infant-outcome information. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

The LactMed extract was bounded, although the displayed sections were not marked truncated; its record was revised December 15, 2025. The MCP lookup notes that missing evidence is not evidence of safety. The MCP also notes that stopping or changing a medication can carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

Application limits:
This LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. Omitted sections or truncation can limit the summary; absence of retrieved findings is not evidence of safety.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Its warning discusses increased risk in the context of renal dysfunction, hypoperfusion or hypoxemia, unstable or acute heart failure, older age, hepatic disease, dehydration, sepsis, excessive alcohol intake, surgery, and intravascular radiocontrast studies. These are warnings about the person taking the medicine; they are not reported infant outcomes. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)\\n\\nThe label\u2019s adult adverse-reaction section reports gastrointestinal reactions, including diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, indigestion, and abdominal discomfort, as well as other reported reactions. They do not test every adult label warning, and they do not establish outcomes for all breastfed infants. In another report, metformin was undetectable in the **serum** of two infants. Infant ages, extent of nursing, sampling details, and other context were not uniformly stated. These are measured exposure findings, not administered doses or treatment instructions. [S32](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)\\n\\n### Comparison\\n\\n| Adult label | Breastfed-infant evidence |\\n|---|---|\\n| Warns about lactic acidosis and lists adult risk contexts such as renal dysfunction, hypoperfusion or hypoxemia, hepatic disease, dehydration, sepsis, and certain procedures or exposures. | The retrieved LactMed passages report the infant observations above; they do not report lactic acidosis as an observed infant outcome. The extract does not establish whether that outcome was assessed in all cited infants. |\\n| Reports adult gastrointestinal adverse reactions and other adult adverse reactions. | The cited infant passages report the specific growth, development, illness, glucose, and adverse-effect observations listed above. They do not establish that the adult gastrointestinal reactions occurred in those infants. |\\n| Describes adult drug-interaction information. | The retrieved LactMed passages do not establish corresponding interaction outcomes in breastfed infants. |\\n\\n### Missing and bounded sections\\n\\n- The DailyMed extraction returned the adult **Warnings**, **Adverse Reactions**, and **Drug Interactions** sections, but **Warnings and Precautions** and **Boxed Warning** were missing in the extracted adult medicine-taker sections. The Warnings text was also truncated. Missing sections are extraction limitations, not evidence that the information is absent from the full label. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)\\n- LactMed returned its expected sections\u2014Summary of Use during Lactation, Drug Levels, Effects in Breastfed Infants, and Effects on Lactation and Breastmilk\u2014with no section marked truncated. However, the study count was **not established in the exported extract**, and the record remains a bounded extract rather than a complete literature review. [S32](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)\\n- The retrieved PubMed search was bounded, not systematic. request.question: Compare metformin label warnings for the adult taking it with findings in breastfed infants. Identify which source says what, and disclose missing sections. Don't give any doses.

response.answer:
## Metformin: adult label warnings compared with breastfed-infant findings

**Source identity:** Metformin was verified as the ingredient reviewed. [S30](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/6809/properties.json)

### Adult taking metformin: what the selected label says

The selected DailyMed product label states that **lactic acidosis** is a rare but serious complication associated with metformin accumulation. Its warning discusses increased risk in the context of renal dysfunction, hypoperfusion or hypoxemia, unstable or acute heart failure, older age, hepatic disease, dehydration, sepsis, excessive alcohol intake, surgery, and intravascular radiocontrast studies. These are warnings about the person taking the medicine; they are not reported infant outcomes. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

The label’s adult adverse-reaction section reports gastrointestinal reactions, including diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, indigestion, and abdominal discomfort, as well as other reported reactions. The retrieved label text does not establish that these adult reactions occurred in breastfed infants. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

### Breastfed infants: what LactMed reports

LactMed reports the following observations in specific lactation populations:

- Seven infants aged **5–25 months** were described as healthy, with growth and development progressing as expected; two had normal Denver developmental screening tests.
- Three infants aged **2, 5, and 14 months** were reported to have no detectable adverse effects in the cited passage.
- In three infants aged **10–11 days postpartum**, none had low blood glucose levels.
- In a reported comparison involving **61 predominantly breastfed and 50 formula-fed infants**, no differences at 3 or 6 months were reported in height, weight, motor-social development, or rates of illness between the groups.

These are observations from the cited LactMed passages in those specific populations. They do not test every adult label warning, and they do not establish outcomes for all breastfed infants. [S32](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

### Measured exposure

LactMed reported these **milk concentrations** in different maternal sampling contexts:

- **270 mcg/L**: average milk level in one group, with levels varying little over 24 hours.
- **380 mcg/L**: an approximately 4–5-hour post-dose milk measurement in one woman.
- **130–270 mcg/L**: average milk levels reported in another group.
- **410 mcg/L**: estimated average milk level in a postpartum sampling study.

Infant-level information was also retrieved: LactMed reports that **serum levels** were measured in four breastfed infants; two measurements were undetectable below the reported threshold, and two were **50 and 80 mcg/L**. In another report, metformin was undetectable in the **serum** of two infants. Infant ages, extent of nursing, sampling details, and other context were not uniformly stated. These are measured exposure findings, not administered doses or treatment instructions. [S32](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

### Comparison

| Adult label | Breastfed-infant evidence |
|---|---|
| Warns about lactic acidosis and lists adult risk contexts such as renal dysfunction, hypoperfusion or hypoxemia, hepatic disease, dehydration, sepsis, and certain procedures or exposures. | The retrieved LactMed passages report the infant observations above; they do not report lactic acidosis as an observed infant outcome. The extract does not establish whether that outcome was assessed in all cited infants. |
| Reports adult gastrointestinal adverse reactions and other adult adverse reactions. | The cited infant passages report the specific growth, development, illness, glucose, and adverse-effect observations listed above. They do not establish that the adult gastrointestinal reactions occurred in those infants. |
| Describes adult drug-interaction information. | The retrieved LactMed passages do not establish corresponding interaction outcomes in breastfed infants. |

### Missing and bounded sections

- The DailyMed extraction returned the adult **Warnings**, **Adverse Reactions**, and **Drug Interactions** sections, but **Warnings and Precautions** and **Boxed Warning** were missing in the extracted adult medicine-taker sections. The Warnings text was also truncated. Missing sections are extraction limitations, not evidence that the information is absent from the full label. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)
- LactMed returned its expected sections—Summary of Use during Lactation, Drug Levels, Effects in Breastfed Infants, and Effects on Lactation and Breastmilk—with no section marked truncated. However, the study count was **not established in the exported extract**, and the record remains a bounded extract rather than a complete literature review. [S32](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)
- The retrieved PubMed search was bounded, not systematic. Abstract text was returned for **4 of 5** requested records; no abstract text was returned for **PMID 38197154**. No outcome finding from that record is used here. [S8](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22metformin%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22metformin%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22metformin%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- FAERS is separate from the LactMed clinical findings. The returned metformin query covered reports matching the query, not a confirmed lactation or infant cohort. Reported terms included nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, lactic acidosis, and acute kidney injury, among others; the returned counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed outcomes, and the source states that causation and incidence cannot be established. The results cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22metformin%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S14](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

The MCP server’s continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician; this is MCP-generated guidance, not a statement from the label or LactMed.

request.question: Is there an FDA-listed pregnancy exposure registry covering topiramate? Give the listing and registry contact or enrollment link if returned, and distinguish finding a registry from being eligible to enroll.

response.answer:
Yes. The FDA directory returned this listing for **topiramate**:

- **Registry:** The North American Antiepileptic Drug in Pregnancy Registry  
- **Listed products:** Topamax, Trokendi XR, Qudexy XR (topiramate)  
- **Conditions listed:** Epilepsy, mood disorder, migraine headaches  
- **Status as listed:** Ongoing  
- **Contact:** Massachusetts General Hospital for Children  
  - **Phone:** 1-888-233-2334  
  - **Enrollment link:** [S1](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)

This is a registry listing, not a determination that any particular person is eligible to enroll. Eligibility and current site availability must be confirmed with the registry team. The FDA directory notes that FDA lists but does not operate or endorse these registries, and that the list is not comprehensive. [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Find up to two recruiting ADHD studies involving children in the United States. Include exact study links, overall and site status if present, update dates, contacts and qualification limits. Do not decide whether a child qualifies.

response.answer:
## Recruiting U.S. ADHD studies involving children

The search returned two unranked potential matches. The source population field is **not established** for both records; the listed age ranges and child designation come from the registry’s eligibility fields. The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability; this lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

### 1. Digital Health Intervention for Children With ADHD — NCT06456372

- **Exact study link:** https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06456372 [S3](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06456372)
- **Study type:** Interventional
- **Overall status:** **RECRUITING**
- **Site status:**  
  - The Craig School, Irvine, California — **RECRUITING**  
  - UCR Psychiatry at Grindstaff Community School, Riverside, California — **RECRUITING**
- **Last update posted:** January 28, 2026
- **Registry age range:** 8–12 years; standard age: CHILD; sex: ALL; healthy volunteers: false
- **Listed qualification limits:**  
  - DSM-5-TR ADHD diagnosis through prior medical or psychological evaluations  
  - Ability to complete questionnaires and use an app in English  
  - Reported IQ of at least 80  
  - Parent/guardian available to consent and provide feedback in English  
  - Exclusion: failure to meet an inclusion criterion
- **Central contacts:**  
  - Jaime Smith — 951-827-0741; jaime.smith@medsch.ucr.edu  
  - Kimberley Lakes — 951-827-2410; kimberley.lakes@medsch.ucr.edu
- **Site contact:** Nancy Herrera, PhD — nancy.herrera@medsch.ucr.edu

### 2. Enhancing Team Effectiveness for a Collaborative School-based Intervention for ADHD — NCT06180681

- **Exact study link:** https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06180681 [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06180681)
- **Study type:** Interventional
- **Overall status:** **RECRUITING**
- **Site status:**  
  - IN STEP Children’s Mental Health Center, San Diego, California — **RECRUITING**
- **Last update posted:** June 30, 2026
- **Registry age range:** 7–11 years; standard age: CHILD; sex: ALL; healthy volunteers: false
- **Listed qualification limits:**  
  - Ages 7–11 years and attendance at a participating school  
  - Referral by a school mental-health provider for apparent ADHD-related problems  
  - Listed parent/teacher symptom and impairment thresholds  
  - Caregiver and teacher consent, plus child assent  
  - Exclusions include certain severe impairments or conditions, all-day special-education classroom placement, inability of the child or caregiver to read or speak English or Spanish, and plans to change psychotropic medication  
  - The record states that children taking medication for attention or behavior may be eligible when their medication regimens are stable
- **Central/site contact:** Lilliana Conradi, BA — 1-619-651-3154; lconradi@health.ucsd.edu

**Search limitations:** This bounded search screened only the first 20 API matches and required literal topic words in the title, conditions, or interventions; synonyms may have been missed. Overall recruitment does not establish that every site recruits, and registry status may be stale. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

Application limits:
The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation.

request.question: Are any recruiting pediatric epilepsy studies returned for Canada? Show up to two with study links and contacts, or clearly explain if the search found none. Do not substitute completed studies.

response.answer:
One recruiting pediatric study was returned for Canada:

### Real World Evidence on the Use of Medical Cannabis in Pediatrics
- **Status:** RECRUITING
- **Study type:** OBSERVATIONAL
- **Source population:** Children aged 3–17 years; the study summary describes children with authorizations for medical cannabis across Canada.
- **Epilepsy relevance:** Epilepsy is listed as a condition, but the registry classifies the match as **indirect/unverified** and does not confirm that the study is specifically for established epilepsy.
- **Canadian site:** U Manitoba, Winnipeg, Manitoba — site status: **RECRUITING**
- **Contact:** Lauren E. Kelly, PhD — lauren.kelly@umanitoba.ca; 2042723149
- **Study link:** https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05863910 [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05863910)

The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This bounded search returned one record; it is not exhaustive, and registry recruitment status may be stale. No completed studies were substituted. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=pediatric+epilepsy+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=Canada)

Application limits:
The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation.

response.answer:
The official FDA page is **FDA MedWatch: report a suspected medicine problem**: [S3](https://www.fda.gov/safety/medwatch-fda-safety-information-and-adverse-event-reporting-program)

A report by itself does **not** establish that the medicine caused the problem. No report was filed.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Find a PubMed paper about levetiracetam while breastfeeding, retrieve its abstract, and summarize only the study design, population and findings actually available. Distinguish drug exposure from infant outcomes.

response.answer:
**Paper:** *Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?* (PMID 34131926) [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Study design and population
- The abstract does not state a formal study-design label. It reports that breastfeeding women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam completed a questionnaire and provided serial breast-milk samples from before administration through 12 hours afterward, plus one pre-administration maternal serum sample.
- The study included **20 women and 21 infants**; one woman had twins. Sixteen infants were fully breastfed and five were partially breastfed.

### Drug exposure
- Levetiracetam was measured in breast milk and maternal serum.
- The reported trough breast-milk/maternal-serum ratio was **0.98 ± 0.20**.
- The abstract reports relative infant exposure estimates of **13.8 ± 3.1%** in fully breastfed infants and **6.9 ± 1.6%** in partially breastfed infants.
- Correlations were reported among maternal levetiracetam exposure, maternal serum concentrations, breast-milk trough concentrations, and breast-milk exposure over time.

### Infant outcomes
- Three women reported somnolence in their fully breastfed infants. The abstract states that this resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding; it does not establish causation.
- The abstract states that all infants gained weight according to age.
- Short- and long-term safety were not established by the abstract; the authors stated that further studies were warranted.

The abstract lookup succeeded for the one requested record. No requested records were missing, unreturned, or failed; this was not a complete literature review.

Application limits:
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: What can infant adverse-event reports involving acetaminophen tell a researcher, and what can they not establish about how often side effects occur or whether the medicine caused them? Use the MCP and state the age scope actually queried.

response.answer:
The MCP queried **FAERS infant reports for acetaminophen** using ages coded in months from **0 through 12 months**; records using other age units were excluded. This is the queried age scope, not a result covering all infants. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)

### What the reports can tell researchers

Within that queried report subset, the returned counts show reported terms such as:

- Off-label use: **135**
- Drug administration error: **121**
- Vomiting: **117**
- Pyrexia: **98**
- Product-use issue: **83**
- Overdose: **77**
- Rash: **60**
- Irritability: **42**
- Seizure: **35**
- Acute hepatic failure: **28**
- Liver injury: **28**

These terms describe spontaneous reports in the query. They can help characterize which events or use-related terms were reported and their reporting volume. The individual result records did not establish a source population or confirm an age band beyond the query filter. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)

### What they cannot establish

- **How often side effects occur:** the query has no exposure denominator, so the counts cannot calculate incidence, rates, or individual risk.
- **Whether acetaminophen caused an event:** the reports do not establish causation.
- **How common an event is among all infants or all infants exposed to acetaminophen:** these results cover only the queried report subset and cannot be generalized to either population.
- **That every returned term is a side effect:** the list includes use-related terms such as off-label use, administration errors, overdose, and product-use issues.
- **That an unlisted event was absent:** the returned list does not establish absence of other reports.

The result was a bounded return of 25 terms, with no continuation supplied; it should not be treated as an exhaustive assessment. These limitations are part of the MCP’s FAERS interpretation and are also documented by openFDA. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25) [S2](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Using the parent medication information tool, summarize the sertraline evidence from LactMed and the product label. Separate measured milk exposure from observed infant outcomes. Include links and questions to ask a clinician. Do not give dosing or medication decisions.

response.answer:
## Sertraline during breastfeeding

The medicine identity was confirmed as **sertraline**. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Measured exposure in breast milk

LactMed reported the following milk concentrations:

- In a pooled analysis of 15 mothers, breast-milk sertraline averaged **45 mcg/L**, with a reported range of **7–207 mcg/L**.
- In 26 women studied with extensive milk and serum sampling over 24 hours, milk sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**) and norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**).
- In four mothers at 2 months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L for sertraline** and **29 mcg/L for norsertraline**, with sampling at random times.
- In a report involving the mother of a preterm infant, milk concentrations at random times averaged **201 mcg/L for sertraline** and **358 mcg/L for norsertraline**.
- One report gave a milk sertraline concentration of **29 mcg/L**; the sampling times were not stated.

These are research measurements, not administered amounts or dosing guidance. The retrieved LactMed extract did **not** contain infant-level concentration data; infant-level information is therefore missing from this extract. The “Drug Levels” section was truncated, so additional source information may not be represented. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

LactMed reported:

request.question: Prepare an evidence brief for sertraline during lactation using the medication evidence brief tool. Include questions to ask my clinician, source links, and missing evidence limitations. Do not provide medication decisions or doses.

response.answer:
## Sertraline during lactation: evidence brief

**Evidence status:** Sertraline was exactly identified as the single ingredient sertraline. The retrieved material is partial and does not determine an individual treatment plan. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Effect on the lactating person

- LactMed reports that a midwife observed **six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline**; administered amounts were not reported in that passage. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In one reported case, a mother reported increased milk supply during a one-week interruption and decreased supply after restarting sertraline. The returned extract does not establish the exact timing of other relevant events or prove causation. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed also reports discussion of galactorrhea and a pharmacovigilance analysis concerning hyperprolactinemia. The complete supporting passages were not returned. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These are source-reported observations, not proof that sertraline caused the effects.

### Measured exposure in milk

The returned LactMed extract reported these milk concentrations:

- **Sertraline:** mean **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**, from a pooled analysis involving 15 mothers. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- **Sertraline:** mean **129 mcg/L**, range **11–938 mcg/L**; **norsertraline:** mean **258 mcg/L**, range **20–1,498 mcg/L**, in a study with extensive milk and maternal-serum sampling over 24 hours. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- At two months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline in four mothers sampled at random times. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a report involving a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline; the returned passage does not provide a complete infant-exposure description. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

**Infant-level information:** No infant-level concentration excerpt was returned. Infant specimen type and the complete infant-level measurement record are therefore missing from this extract. Milk concentrations are research measurements, not dose instructions.

### Observed infant outcomes

- One report described benign neonatal sleep myoclonus in a four-month-old infant and agitation that reportedly resolved spontaneously. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a separate group of 26 infants, the returned passage reported no detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breast milk. The returned summary does not provide the complete study context. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of 14 mothers and their breastfed infants, whole-blood serotonin measurements were obtained after maternal therapy. The passage reports infant serotonin averages before and after therapy and the authors’ interpretation concerning platelet serotonin uptake. This is an observed laboratory finding from that study, not an individual prediction. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The retrieved extract includes additional infant-outcome material, but the **Effects in Breastfed Infants** section was truncated. The underlying study count and complete study designs were not established from this extract. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### FAERS report-only context

The FDA spontaneous-report query returned these top terms and counts:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Nausea | 14,075 |
| Drug ineffective | 13,855 |
| Fatigue | 13,021 |
| Headache | 11,284 |
| Anxiety | 10,530 |
| Diarrhea | 10,499 |
| Dizziness | 9,741 |
| Depression | 9,612 |

The query covered reports matching sertraline in an **any-population report subset**, not a confirmed lactation or infant cohort. These counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; they do not establish causation and lack exposure denominators. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Label context

The selected DailyMed product was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**. The retrieved label included a standalone **“8.2 Lactation”** entry, but the tool identified a title/code mismatch requiring verification. The lactation section was not truncated; the pregnancy section was truncated. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The retrieved medicine-taker section listed adverse reactions and warnings including hypersensitivity reactions, serotonin syndrome, increased bleeding risk, activation of mania/hypomania, discontinuation syndrome, seizures, angle-closure glaucoma, hyponatremia, and sexual dysfunction. Other expected adult warning sections were missing from the returned extract; that is an extraction limitation, not evidence that the full label lacks them. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Literature-retrieval limitations

The search was bounded and returned five PubMed records; it was not a systematic review. Abstract text was retrieved for **3 of 5** requested records. No abstract text was returned for **PMID 38133585** or **PMID 32320387**. No records were unreturned, and no abstract lookups failed. Missing abstracts are retrieval limitations, not evidence that the studies or other research do not exist. Titles alone were not used to describe outcomes. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)

The LactMed **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated in the returned extract. The brief therefore cannot establish the complete evidence base, complete infant-level exposure data, or the full context of all reported outcomes. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Questions to ask your clinician

1. Does this evidence apply to my exact product, formulation, and all active ingredients?
2. How closely do these study populations match my lactation context and my infant’s age or prematurity?
3. Which findings measure milk or infant exposure, and which are observed clinical outcomes?
4. How should the reported milk-supply observations be interpreted in the context of my underlying condition and other factors affecting lactation?

Use the evidence brief tool.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Questions to ask your clinician\\n\\n1. Does the available evidence apply to my exact sertraline product and formulation?\\n2. How closely do the study populations match my breastfeeding situation, including my infant\u2019s age, health, and prematurity status?\\n3. Which findings measure sertraline exposure, and which describe observed infant outcomes?\\n4. What do the reported milk concentrations mean for my individual circumstances?\\n5. What infant-level measurements were collected, and which information is missing from the retrieved evidence?\\n6. How should the isolated reports of infant sleep myoclonus and transient agitation be interpreted in context?\\n7. How should the reports of decreased milk supply be interpreted, and what other information would be needed to assess my situation?\\n8. What uncertainties remain because some LactMed sections were truncated and the literature search was bounded rather than systematic?\\n9. What benefits, risks, and follow-up considerations should we discuss together before making a treatment decision?\\n10. If treatment changes are being considered, what should we discuss about continuity of care?\\n\\n## Brief evidence context\\n\\n### Effect on the lactating person\\n\\nLactMed describes reports involving galactorrhea and reports from six patients of decreased milk supply after starting sertraline. The retrieved extract does not establish how applicable these reports are to an individual situation. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n\\nRetrieved LactMed milk measurements included:\\n\\n- **Sertraline:** 45 mcg/L, with a reported range of 7\u2013207 mcg/L, in a pooled analysis of 15 mothers.\\n- **Sertraline:** average 129 mcg/L, range 11\u2013938 mcg/L, in a study of 26 breastfeeding women.\\n- **Norsertraline:** average 258 mcg/L, range 20\u20131,498 mcg/L, in that same study.\\n- Additional reported milk measurements included sertraline at 26.4 mcg/L and norsertraline at 29 mcg/L in four mothers, and other study-specific measurements with sampling times described as random or not stated.\\n\\nThese are measured research concentrations, not administered amounts or individualized treatment guidance. The retrieved infant-level concentration excerpt was missing; the source does not establish infant specimen details from this extract. The LactMed **Drug Levels** section was truncated, so the extract is incomplete. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\nThe retrieved LactMed extract reports one 4-month-old infant with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation in the context of maternal sertraline use. It also reports a group of 26 infants in which no detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breastmilk were reported. These are separate source findings from different reports and populations; they do not determine an individual infant\u2019s outcome. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### FAERS report context\\n\\nThe retrieved FAERS query covered reports matching sertraline in a broad, unspecified population, not a confirmed breastfeeding or infant cohort. Reported terms included nausea (14,075), \u201cdrug ineffective\u201d (13,855), fatigue (13,021), headache (11,284), anxiety (10,530), diarrhoea (10,499), dizziness (9,741), and depression (9,612). These are reporting volumes, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; the query had no exposure denominator and does not establish causation or generalize to all infants or exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)\\n\\n### Retrieval limitations\\n\\nThe retrieved PubMed set contained five records. Abstract text was available for three; no abstract text was returned for PMID 38133585 and PMID 32320387. Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, and titles alone were not used to describe outcomes. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)\\n\\nThe LactMed record also states that its Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections were truncated, so this should not be treated as a complete evidence review. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nApplication limits:\\nThese FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.\\nHuman clinical framing review remains required. request.question: Please prepare questions for my clinician about the evidence for sertraline during breastfeeding. Use the evidence brief tool.

response.answer:
## Questions to ask your clinician

1. Does the available evidence apply to my exact sertraline product and formulation?
2. How closely do the study populations match my breastfeeding situation, including my infant’s age, health, and prematurity status?
3. Which findings measure sertraline exposure, and which describe observed infant outcomes?
4. What do the reported milk concentrations mean for my individual circumstances?
5. What infant-level measurements were collected, and which information is missing from the retrieved evidence?
6. How should the isolated reports of infant sleep myoclonus and transient agitation be interpreted in context?
7. How should the reports of decreased milk supply be interpreted, and what other information would be needed to assess my situation?
8. What uncertainties remain because some LactMed sections were truncated and the literature search was bounded rather than systematic?
9. What benefits, risks, and follow-up considerations should we discuss together before making a treatment decision?
10. If treatment changes are being considered, what should we discuss about continuity of care?

## Brief evidence context

### Effect on the lactating person

LactMed describes reports involving galactorrhea and reports from six patients of decreased milk supply after starting sertraline. The retrieved extract does not establish how applicable these reports are to an individual situation. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure

Retrieved LactMed milk measurements included:

- **Sertraline:** 45 mcg/L, with a reported range of 7–207 mcg/L, in a pooled analysis of 15 mothers.
- **Sertraline:** average 129 mcg/L, range 11–938 mcg/L, in a study of 26 breastfeeding women.
- **Norsertraline:** average 258 mcg/L, range 20–1,498 mcg/L, in that same study.
- Additional reported milk measurements included sertraline at 26.4 mcg/L and norsertraline at 29 mcg/L in four mothers, and other study-specific measurements with sampling times described as random or not stated.

These are measured research concentrations, not administered amounts or individualized treatment guidance. The retrieved infant-level concentration excerpt was missing; the source does not establish infant specimen details from this extract. The LactMed **Drug Levels** section was truncated, so the extract is incomplete. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

The retrieved LactMed extract reports one 4-month-old infant with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation in the context of maternal sertraline use. It also reports a group of 26 infants in which no detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breastmilk were reported. These are separate source findings from different reports and populations; they do not determine an individual infant’s outcome. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### FAERS report context

The retrieved FAERS query covered reports matching sertraline in a broad, unspecified population, not a confirmed breastfeeding or infant cohort. Reported terms included nausea (14,075), “drug ineffective” (13,855), fatigue (13,021), headache (11,284), anxiety (10,530), diarrhoea (10,499), dizziness (9,741), and depression (9,612). These are reporting volumes, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; the query had no exposure denominator and does not establish causation or generalize to all infants or exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Retrieval limitations

The retrieved PubMed set contained five records. Abstract text was available for three; no abstract text was returned for PMID 38133585 and PMID 32320387. Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, and titles alone were not used to describe outcomes. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)

The LactMed record also states that its Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections were truncated, so this should not be treated as a complete evidence review. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

[S21](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json)\\n\\n**Evidence scope:** This is a bounded evidence summary, not a systematic review. The retrieved PubMed records had abstract text available, with no failed, unreturned, or no-abstract records among the requested records; the search itself was not complete. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)\\n\\n### Effects on the pregnant person\\n\\nThe retrieved material includes disease- and treatment-context information for epilepsy, but it does not provide a quantified, lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome estimate.\\n\\nThe selected label describes pregnancy-associated changes in lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect. It also discusses maternal and fetal risks associated with epilepsy and poorly controlled convulsive seizures; these passages are not measurements of a lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nA review passage retrieved from *Management of epilepsy during pregnancy and lactation* discusses valproate, not lamotrigine, so it should not be used as a lamotrigine maternal-effect finding. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)\\n\\n**Gap:** The selected label\u2019s adult medicine-taker sections\u2014adverse reactions, warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug interactions\u2014were missing from the retrieved extract. ## Pregnancy evidence brief: lamotrigine

**Identity:** The retrieved record matched lamotrigine as a single active ingredient. [S21](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json)

**Evidence scope:** This is a bounded evidence summary, not a systematic review. The retrieved PubMed records had abstract text available, with no failed, unreturned, or no-abstract records among the requested records; the search itself was not complete. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

### Effects on the pregnant person

The retrieved material includes disease- and treatment-context information for epilepsy, but it does not provide a quantified, lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome estimate.

The selected label describes pregnancy-associated changes in lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect. It also discusses maternal and fetal risks associated with epilepsy and poorly controlled convulsive seizures; these passages are not measurements of a lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A review passage retrieved from *Management of epilepsy during pregnancy and lactation* discusses valproate, not lamotrigine, so it should not be used as a lamotrigine maternal-effect finding. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)

**Gap:** The selected label’s adult medicine-taker sections—adverse reactions, warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug interactions—were missing from the retrieved extract. Missing sections do not establish absence of information or safety. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Fetal exposure

#### Maternal pharmacokinetics

The label’s Clinical Considerations states that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect. It reports decreased lamotrigine concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. The retrieved passage does not provide the underlying study sizes, sampling times, concentration values, or study designs. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A review states that physiological changes during pregnancy affect antiseizure-medication levels and seizure risk. In the retrieved passage, the population and study design for a lamotrigine-specific finding were not established. [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)

A naturalistic study of **60 mothers** measured psychopharmacological medications in serum and breastmilk at different time points and followed exposed children during the first 12 months. Its abstract reports a high concentration-by-dose ratio in breastmilk for lamotrigine. This is lactation-related exposure information, not a measured fetal concentration, and the retrieved abstract does not provide lamotrigine-specific concentration values, units, sampling times, or infant specimen results. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

No verified fetal concentration was retrieved in this brief.

### Fetal outcomes

The selected label reports findings from pregnancy registries involving lamotrigine monotherapy exposure during the first trimester:

- The International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry reported major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558 infants**, with a reported 95% confidence interval of **1.6%–3.1%**.
- The NAAED Pregnancy Registry reported major congenital malformations among **2.0%** of **1,562 infants**.
- In a separate NAAED analysis of **2,200 infants** exposed early in pregnancy, isolated oral clefts were reported at **3.2 per 1,000**, with a reported 95% confidence interval of **1.4–6.3** and a reported comparison with unexposed healthy controls.

These are separate registry findings reported in the label. The label states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions that can be drawn. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label also states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. Results for those outcomes were not included in the retrieved summary, so they are not established here. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

Animal findings in the label, including fetal folate changes, are animal data and are not human fetal outcomes. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### FAERS report-only context

For the retrieved query of lamotrigine reports containing the reaction term **“foetal exposure during pregnancy,”** FAERS returned these reporting volumes:

- Foetal exposure during pregnancy: **3,527**
- Atrial septal defect: **357**
- Congenital anomaly: **327**
- Premature baby: **257**
- Ventricular septal defect: **205**
- Patent ductus arteriosus: **153**
- Spina bifida: **143**
- Hypospadias: **135**

The query covered reports matching the stated terms, not a complete exposed population. The source population was not confirmed for every report, exposure denominators were unavailable, and the returned counts are reporting volume—not incidence, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to lamotrigine. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S12](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

[S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4) [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)
- The retrieved lactation study did not provide lamotrigine-specific concentration values, units, sampling times, or infant specimen results in the available abstract. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

{"answer": "## Pregnancy evidence brief: lamotrigine

**Identity:** The retrieved record matched lamotrigine as a single active ingredient. [S21](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json)

**Evidence scope:** This is a bounded evidence summary, not a systematic review. The retrieved PubMed records had abstract text available, with no failed, unreturned, or no-abstract records among the requested records; the search itself was not complete. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

### Effects on the pregnant person

The retrieved material includes disease- and treatment-context information for epilepsy, but it does not provide a quantified, lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome estimate.

The selected label describes pregnancy-associated changes in lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect. It also discusses maternal and fetal risks associated with epilepsy and poorly controlled convulsive seizures; these passages are not measurements of a lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A review passage retrieved from *Management of epilepsy during pregnancy and lactation* discusses valproate, not lamotrigine, so it should not be used as a lamotrigine maternal-effect finding. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)

**Gap:** The selected label’s adult medicine-taker sections—adverse reactions, warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug interactions—were missing from the retrieved extract. Missing sections do not establish absence of information or safety. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Fetal exposure

#### Maternal pharmacokinetics

The label’s Clinical Considerations states that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect. It reports decreased lamotrigine concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. The retrieved passage does not provide the underlying study sizes, sampling times, concentration values, or study designs. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A review states that physiological changes during pregnancy affect antiseizure-medication levels and seizure risk. In the retrieved passage, the population and study design for a lamotrigine-specific finding were not established. [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)

A naturalistic study of **60 mothers** measured psychopharmacological medications in serum and breastmilk at different time points and followed exposed children during the first 12 months. Its abstract reports a high concentration-by-dose ratio in breastmilk for lamotrigine. This is lactation-related exposure information, not a measured fetal concentration, and the retrieved abstract does not provide lamotrigine-specific concentration values, units, sampling times, or infant specimen results. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

No verified fetal concentration was retrieved in this brief.

### Fetal outcomes

The selected label reports findings from pregnancy registries involving lamotrigine monotherapy exposure during the first trimester:

- The International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry reported major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558 infants**, with a reported 95% confidence interval of **1.6%–3.1%**.
- The NAAED Pregnancy Registry reported major congenital malformations among **2.0%** of **1,562 infants**.
- In a separate NAAED analysis of **2,200 infants** exposed early in pregnancy, isolated oral clefts were reported at **3.2 per 1,000**, with a reported 95% confidence interval of **1.4–6.3** and a reported comparison with unexposed healthy controls.

These are separate registry findings reported in the label. The label states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions that can be drawn. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label also states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. Results for those outcomes were not included in the retrieved summary, so they are not established here. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

Animal findings in the label, including fetal folate changes, are animal data and are not human fetal outcomes. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### FAERS report-only context

For the retrieved query of lamotrigine reports containing the reaction term **“foetal exposure during pregnancy,”** FAERS returned these reporting volumes:

- Foetal exposure during pregnancy: **3,527**
- Atrial septal defect: **357**
- Congenital anomaly: **327**
- Premature baby: **257**
- Ventricular septal defect: **205**
- Patent ductus arteriosus: **153**
- Spina bifida: **143**
- Hypospadias: **135**

The query covered reports matching the stated terms, not a complete exposed population. The source population was not confirmed for every report, exposure denominators were unavailable, and the returned counts are reporting volume—not incidence, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to lamotrigine. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S12](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Evidence gaps

- The pregnancy section of the selected label was truncated in the retrieved extract. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- The maternal pharmacokinetic passages did not provide underlying study designs, sample sizes for the pregnancy concentration observations, gestational timing, or numeric concentration results. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4) [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)
- The retrieved lactation study did not provide lamotrigine-specific concentration values, units, sampling times, or infant specimen results in the available abstract. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)
- Registry findings, FAERS reports, and animal findings are different evidence types and should not be combined.
- The retrieved evidence does not determine an individual pregnancy benefit–risk balance.

The MCP-generated pregnancy coverage notice states that its prototype source review did not identify a curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed; this is a source-review limitation, not proof that no such resource exists. Pregnancy evidence in this retrieval came from product labeling and literature. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4) [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S24](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S25](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

response.answer:
## Sertraline during lactation

Sertraline was exactly matched as the ingredient sertraline (RxNorm 36437). [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Effects reported in lactating people

LactMed reports:

- A midwife observed **six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline**; administered amounts were not reported. This is a report of patient observations, not proof of causation.
- In one explicitly described case, a mother reported increased milk supply during a one-week period when she was not taking sertraline, followed by decreased supply after restarting it. The retrieved passage does not establish that sertraline caused the change.
- LactMed also describes galactorrhea reports in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients. A French pharmacovigilance-center comparison reported that sertraline was not associated with an increased risk of hyperprolactinemia compared with other medicines. The relevance of those findings to established lactation is not fully established in the returned extract.

These findings come from small reports and pharmacovigilance material. The LactMed extract does not establish the number of unique studies, and the full section was not returned. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure in milk

The retrieved LactMed **Drug Levels** section reported:

- In a pooled analysis involving **15 mothers**, mean breast-milk sertraline concentration was **45 mcg/L**, with a range of **7–207 mcg/L**.
- In a study of **26 women** who were breastfeeding, all milk samples contained detectable sertraline: mean **129 mcg/L**, range **11–938 mcg/L**. Norsertraline was also detected: mean **258 mcg/L**, range **20–1,498 mcg/L**.

No treatment decisions.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence\\n\\nLamotrigine identity was confirmed as the single ingredient lamotrigine. [S21](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json)\\n\\n### Maternal effects and underlying disease\\n\\nThe selected DailyMed label states that epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-medication exposure, has been associated with preeclampsia, preterm labor, antepartum and postpartum hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. It states that maternal or fetal injury may be greatest with untreated or poorly controlled convulsive seizures. These are label-described risks associated with the underlying disease context; they are not presented as lamotrigine-specific adverse-event estimates. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nThe label also states that pregnancy-related physiological changes may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reports of decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. The retrieved extract does not provide numerical concentration changes or enough study detail to characterize the magnitude or consistency of this finding. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nNo lamotrigine-specific maternal adverse-effect estimate was retrieved in this brief. The selected label\u2019s medicine-taker adverse-reaction and warning sections were missing from extraction; this is an extraction limitation, not evidence that such effects were absent. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\n### Fetal or infant exposure\\n\\nNo verified human fetal concentration or placental-transfer measurement was retrieved.\\n\\nA study of **60 mothers** measured psychotropic-medication concentrations in serum and breastmilk at different time points and followed exposed children during their first 12 months. Its abstract reported a high breastmilk concentration-by-dose ratio for lamotrigine. This is lactation-related exposure evidence, not a fetal concentration measurement; the retrieved abstract did not provide a numeric lamotrigine concentration, units, sampling times, or infant specimen results. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)\\n\\nThe label reports animal findings in pregnant rats involving decreased fetal folate concentrations. This is animal evidence and is kept separate from human pregnancy outcomes. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\n### Fetal and infant outcomes\\n\\nThe selected label reports:\\n\\n- The International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry reported major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558** infants exposed to lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester; 95% CI, 1.6%\u20133.1%.\\n- The North American Antiepileptic Drug (NAAED) Pregnancy Registry reported major congenital malformations in **2.0%** of **1,562** infants exposed to lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester.\\n- In a NAAED analysis of **2,200** infants exposed early in pregnancy, isolated oral clefts were reported at **3.2 per 1,000**; the label describes this as a threefold increase compared with unexposed healthy controls.\\n\\nThe label states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions that can be drawn. It also states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay, but the retrieved extract does not provide their numerical results. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nThe PubMed retrieval included reviews and a practice guideline, but the summarized material does not establish additional lamotrigine-specific outcome estimates from those records. The search was bounded rather than systematic. All eight requested PubMed records had abstract text returned; none were reported as missing, unreturned, or failed abstract lookups. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/) [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35133310/) [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/) [S19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38748979/)\\n\\n### FAERS report-only context\\n\\nThe queried FAERS subset returned:\\n\\n- fetal exposure during pregnancy: **3,527 reports**\\n- atrial septal defect: **357**\\n- congenital anomaly: **327**\\n- premature baby: **257**\\n- ventricular septal defect: **205**\\n- patent ductus arteriosus: **153**\\n- spina bifida: **143**\\n- hypospadias: **135**\\n\\nThese are reporting volumes from reports matching the query, not confirmed clinical outcomes or incidence rates. The query had no exposure denominator, does not establish causation, and cannot be generalized to all exposed pregnancies, infants, or people exposed to lamotrigine. The queried source population was not confirmed as complete. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S12](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)\\n\\n### Key limitations\\n\\n- The evidence brief used one selected product label, not all lamotrigine formulations. The label was effective October 12, 2026; DailyMed notes that in-use labeling can differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n- The pregnancy section was truncated, and the selected label\u2019s medicine-taker adverse-reaction and warning sections were missing from extraction. [S8](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n- Registry findings concern particular exposure definitions and populations; the retrieved material does not establish applicability to every formulation, co-exposure, indication, timing pattern, or underlying disease.\\n- LactMed was not applicable because the requested population was pregnancy. The MCP\u2019s pregnancy-coverage notice states that its prototype review did not identify a curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed; pregnancy evidence here came from product labeling and literature, and coverage is not exhaustive. [S25](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/) [S24](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule)\\n- The retrieved evidence is not a safety verdict and cannot determine an individual benefit\u2013risk balance.\\n\\n### Questions for the clinician\\n\\n- Which registry population and comparator best match the specific exposure, timing, indication, and co-medications?\\n- How should the underlying condition and risks associated with uncontrolled disease be considered alongside the pregnancy-outcome findings?\\n- Which available findings are measured exposure data, and which are observed clinical outcomes?\\n- What information is missing because of the truncated label and unavailable numerical pharmacokinetic details?\\n- How should the label\u2019s reported pregnancy-related concentration changes be interpreted for this clinical context?\\n\\nThe MCP\u2019s continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. This is MCP-generated guidance, not a statement from the label or literature. Human clinical framing review remains required; this summary is not clinical validation.\\n\\nApplication limits:\\nThese FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.\\nHuman clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.\\nStopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician.
